full_text:
This interview was difficult to transcribe due to background noise on construction site where interview took place.

Interviewer:	Ok, when did you start on the placement?

Subject:	I started in, June. I started last year.

Interviewer:	So you’ve been there quite a while?

Subject:	Yeah, I’ve been for a while. 

Interviewer:	Now can you tell me a bit about [company] and what they do? 

Subject:	Erm 

Interviewer:	Are they just a construction company?

Subject:	No they’re project management company. (Right) So they erm manage or like other little erm, construction companies or sub-contractors. (Okay) So they just manage how everything works out of planning and the buildings, etcetera. So they don’t own the actual construction company. (Yeah) So management, it’s like a management company, as well.

Interviewer:	Okay. And how would you describe the company’s attitude to women? 

Subject:	Are you going to write this down?

Interviewer:	It’s recording. 

Subject:	Do you think they will ever be able to read this? 

Interviewer:	No. 

Subject:	It’s okay. 

Interviewer:	Everything in the reports will be anonymous.

Subject:	Yeah, do that. Erm it’s half and half. Erm some of them are a bit erm ancient. And er some of them are very modern.

Interviewer:	Okay we’ll talk about that more later on. How useful do you think that your course has been to the work that you are doing now?

Subject:	Very useful (Yeah) You can’t, you can’t erm do my degree without doing placement. Definitely not. Unless you have started your degree and you were already working er, if you haven’t done anything before, if you’re eight - eighteen or something like that, you have to have a placement.

Interviewer:	Are you using the skills that you’ve learnt at uni on the placement?

Subject:	No. No. 

Interviewer:	It’s totally different? 

Subject:	I’m not sure I’ve used anything. I know what everything means, that I have learnt and I have done all my coursework on. But, erm other than that, not really. 

Interviewer:	So does that make you think what you’re doing at uni is a waste of time? Or do you still think it’s useful? 

Subject:	Yes, it’s a waste of time. I know like, yeah like the, them, when they’re. Was it the drawing erm modules, where we did sections and elevations - that’s quite useful, cos’ I know what they look like now, so I don’t have my, total no idea of what it looks like. Erm there’s that. And there’s something like erm desire to (inaudible) and you like try and remember what are the trades people do and some of that, er that’s useless. Some of them are quite useless. It’s like CAD is very important. Erm the drawing one’s pretty important. The surveying one was absolutely rubbish. There’s no point even doing that module whatsoever. Yes so it’s like some of them, it’s just, as to know what I was talking about. There was, there was, I mean am I rushing? I was like taking out books, but I don’t know if he was actually writing my correct mark. (Yeah) But it’s now, one (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Yeah. Is there anything like you wished you’d learnt at Uni instead that would have helped you on the placement? 

Subject:	No. Erm. I don’t know. No I don’t think so. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Were you taught anything about Health and Safety at Uni?

Subject:	Yes. 

Interviewer:	Was that helpful or not?

Subject:	Er yeah it is. It is very helpful. Because you always say oh construction’s very (inaudible)and (inaudible). They say that every single time you come to lesson, so, yeah but other than that all boring. (inaudible) most of it anyway.

Interviewer:	Have you had loads of health and safety stuff to do here? 

Subject:	Yeah. You have to wear hard hats and it’s very important. I’ve been hit on the head quite a few times. And if I didn’t erm wear my hard hat I would probably be half dead now. And there I mean, I’ve been bumping into like scaffolding so many times. So, and there’s like, disease and all that. (Yeah) And you catch things and if you don’t wash you hands, er like ten times a day, you can catch something. So. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that University could have done more to prepare you for the placement or do you think you just have to get out there and experience it?

Subject:	I think, yeah. I mean like I was, I’m pretty young, I think. And I wasn’t like very confident when I started. And I don’t think you can do anything about that in uni anyway. So for that, you have to just get out there and do it. Although all the young people; they’re half people there in my class anyway, they’re older. (Yeah) And they had more, like experience anyway. Erm probably, I don’t know, have maybe more CAD. You know the CAD was, was pretty good. It’s just erm, more explanations on what the drawings actually mean for some of them, half of them, some of them, that’s all. 

Interviewer:	Okay. How did you find the transition from being in education to coming to work? Was it easy or difficult? 

Subject:	It was very difficult. I hate getting up really early because I’m so used to getting, getting up really late and sleeping in and everything. 

Interviewer:	What time did you have to start work? 

Subject:	I have to get up at twenty past six. I leave at seven. Start half past seven or eight o’clock. And erm you have no social life. The money’s good. I was probably working in sort of. Down here, I’m only working because of the money, yeah. (inaudible) because I haven’t seen friends. (Yeah) You know. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Are you looking forward to going back to Uni then?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	Why’s that?

Subject:	Because I’ve got my dissertation, which is really hard. (Yeah) And, (inaudible). Erm other than that I’ll see some of my friends more. Erm (inaudible)Although actually I’ve got ten courseworks to do. As for me, so less stress and everything. If you’re working, you go home and forget work. You’ve got nothing to do, it makes (inaudible). Nothing else can be done. And you just, relax, but then uni, you’ve got loads to do all the time. 

Interviewer:	So do you think what you’re doing here will help you at all doing work? 

Subject:	I think, erm I don’t know. I have to get back used to doing my coursework, that’s going to be hard, because I haven’t done it for a year. I will know what I’m talking about, and that’s (inaudible) and everything and maybe I’ll be able to write my coursework with more, clearly (inaudible) at least I’ll know what I’m talking about. 

Interviewer:	Okay, how do you think that work and uni differ? What are the main ways that work and uni differ?

Subject:	Erm it is, it is very different. Working has a, has more responsible, there’s more responsibility in work. There’s so much responsibility. And in Uni, you don’t have any responsibility whatever. And you know if you have a lot of course work, and you’ve got a lot of work to, they say you can do whatever you want, whenever you want. Erm.

Interviewer:	Do you think that they have different goals and priorities? 

Subject:	Yeah. I think, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	That’s okay.

Subject:	Erm.

Interviewer:	Has [company] got many women working for them then?

Subject:	No. Well there’s erm, there is receptionists. That’s two. Me, erm another girl, another girl, (QS?) Yeah. And then there’s like one receptionist for a client, but that doesn’t matter. That’s not a proper. So that’s, so there’s all the management, and they’ve got, theyy’ve got between [inaudible] thirty people. And there’s six girls. But then there’s one QS, which is really high. (Yeah) There’s one in engineering and there’s another one on the (finishes?) there’s me. Erm and then there’s two receptionists. (Okay) So it’s okay, but they should have more. You’re not treated exactly the same as everyone else, that’s why. 

Interviewer:	You don’t think that you are?

Subject:	Yeah. Which we can, I can half use to my advantage because the guys don’t always say no to me. (Yeah) But er, (inaudible). And there’s about er people who talk down to you like you were in University, they do talk down to you. 

Interviewer:	Like they don’t think you’re going to know what you’re talking about?

Subject:	Yes, so they go like, ‘there’s a good girl’, it really pisses me off. (Yeah) And then erm some of the guys got my job. I have to be really harsh and I have to, the only the way people like me get on with that and, they think I’m very, very annoying. I want to know (inaudible). And it’s er, oh she’s a girl, whereas if it was a guy they’ll be snap your fingers and they do it instantly. Erm and some of them are really old thinking. You know but then some of them are really like er, up to date, type thing.
Interviewer:	Okay. Can you give me any examples of when you think being a woman’s determined reactions you’ve got from people or the outcome of any events? 

Subject:	What, sorry?

Interviewer:	Is it just the labourers and stuff that you think there is a gender thing going on, or is it with your colleagues as well?

Subject:	Some of them are old labourers like they say they’re all thinking about some of them and things like that. I mean the younger ones don’t. But then, you know it also doesn’t work. Like (inaudible) And you’re really suppose in the house, like cleaning up and doing the house keeping and you look after the kids. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. They actually say stuff like.

Subject:	Yes, they actually say it to me. I mean and they were very polite at the beginning. (inaudible) after their tease, all of that. Then now, it’s just like, you have to have a really erm, like strong will, kind of thing, you have to be really strong. You can’t be emotional, anything like that. You have to be like very good at taking insults. I mean I get teased a lot. Not like erm horrible teasing, like er teasing on purpose to bully you. But a playful thing. And you have to be full of (inaudible). You have to be really strong, and like especially you take everything so seriously. Er, erm some of the old, I don’t know. Some of the management are mostly (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Have [company] got a structure or programme in place for you to follow as a placement student?

Subject:	Yeah they’ve got like a (inaudible) system. And then erm everyone spends a time in each section. Cos I’m, I’m only for a year, we have two sections. I was in (engineering?) first and now I’m in the (finishings?) department, of construction management. (Okay) Er if I was, here like if they employed me as a trainee, I’d be spending like six to eight months in every single (work that is done?)

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s a good idea to do that? 

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility? 

Subject:	Yes. 

Interviewer:	Not too much or too little? 

Subject:	Yeah. Erm. Erm sometimes erm, sometimes, I don’t know at the beginning it was too little. But now it’s (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Do you feel like they’ve been supportive of you? As like a new recruit or placement student?

Subject:	Erm yeah. Yeah I do. 

Interviewer:	How would you summarise your placement experience so far?

Subject:	 (inaudible)

Interviewer:	How do you react to stuff like that like that, do you give them it back, or?

Subject:	Usually it’s just like a (inaudible) you know, give it back as good as you get. I think they don’t expect it as much. They can tell them about (inaudible) all the girls and (inaudible) wouldn’t to (inaudible). Because I (inaudible) but you know. 

Interviewer:	 (inaudible)

Subject:	Yeah. But they’re eighteen year old’s. And I’m like twenty-two (inaudible). But it’s been good though, yeah it’s been very good, you feel, you know, to get a job afterwards. But it is very different from uni work. You don’t even know what you’re doing because, when you’re doing a placement. (inaudible) You have no idea (inaudible) a few months to get to use work (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Would you recommend other people to do a placement?

Subject:	Yeah. Definitely. 

Interviewer:	Has the placement met your expectations?

Subject:	Erm yeah. I mean, I’m trying to think what it was in the beginning. I was very like sort of half nervous, have scared in the beginning. Erm er yeah it has. 

Interviewer:	What would you said had been the best and the worst things about the placement?

Subject:	Erm there erm. What can I say the worst things are, is the whole teasing and everything and if you, if you not very, I wasn’t very confident. And I was a very little shy and everything at the beginning. I think that’s like, it’s not good to be like that. You have to (grow up?) pretty quickly. And sometimes I feel well, I feel a little bit scared of asking things, and you have to get over that very quickly as well. Erm it’s just mainly the teasing I think. Well like when they, I don’t know it’s like, it’s - it’s only playful in a way, they don’t mean it, but you have to like, you can’t get stressed, you know you have to go on and pretend that nothing bothers you, you have to be that kind of person. (Yeah) I think that’s the bad one, and waking up really early, which I really, really hate. I’m not a nice person when I wake up. My boyfriend says to me, you go away, you better change your job you know. You were in such a bad mood when you wake up. And I say, well I’ll wake up and say, oh I got to go to work, and I can’t wait til friday. And then weekend comes and it’s over very quickly. (Yeah) Erm and the good thing, oh and the bad thing. When you work outside, you have to be used to the cold. Working outside, I hate it. Er the good, the good thing is erm, it prepares you for erm when you actually go, finish the degree and you want to get a job, and you like, you know exactly what it’s like, coming to work and you, you’ve learnt like every company’s a little bit different. You know exactly how they are generally run, and how everything generally is, and what you do and stuff like that. 

Interviewer:	Has the teasing and that decreased as time goes on, or is it just the same?

Subject:	No it started with like er, really nothing, really less of it, and like. I mean only being funny, yeah? (Yeah) Erm and it’s got more and more. I don’t know. I think it’s got. Yes some of them will have more, some, some of the guys on site are like polite and nice. But some of them are really, just doesn’t give you a good impression of those guys, some of them. 

Interviewer:	 (inaudible)

Subject:	No. There’s, you’ve just got to take it, that’s why. But some of them are really, really bad. And then, you know, when they go home, they’re really different towards their wives. And this is like oh, working, you know. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Are there any other students on placement here?

Subject:	Yeah. He’s some graduate from [university] here. There’s like erm, one, two, including me, three, four. It’s quite a lot actually, it’s something like (inaudible). Something like that. 

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s a good thing having other students on placement or don’t you have much to do with them? 

Subject:	Oh no, I think it’s a good thing, so you know it’s not working (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you feel like you’re treated the same as a permanent member staff?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	Is that because you’re a placement student? 

Subject:	You’re only here for (inaudible) months (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Do you have to do much team work?

Subject:	Erm yes. 

Interviewer:	And how do you think that compares to doing team work at uni? 

Subject:	Erm it’s a little bit the same, you know. It’s just at uni it’s with, it depends who you’re with. If you’re not with your friends, then you can sort of get away with not doing anything. Or doing a little bit. Whereas here you to do your share as well. You have to do it otherwise it doesn’t get done. And (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Okay erm are there any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with? 

Subject:	Erm I’ll tell you later (other people are in the room)

Interviewer:	Have you been given a mentor at all?

Subject:	 (We asked for scheme mentors?) Erm that’s only like recently, they’ve starting doing that. Erm I think when maybe, I have one in a month’s time or two. Yeah it’s like someone you’re supposed to erm speak to about anything, that you worry about or if anyone’s bothering you or …

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s a good idea? 

Subject:	Half and half. It depends who it is. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. 

Subject:	I mean, yeah it depends whether there is one. 

Interviewer:	Do you know who you’re getting yet?

Subject:	No I don’t know. But I’m not bothered, I’m not really here for that, so it doesn’t really bother me that much. And now I will speak, (inaudible) speak anyway. I’d probably speak to someone else.

Interviewer:	Has anyone from Uni been to visit you yet?

Subject:	Erm yeah my lecturer hass. Like erm [placement tutor]. (Yeah) Yeah he’s come to visit me. He is coming with me again actually. You know, yeah I think maybe it was before christmas for a review and also [company] does reviews as well. (Yeah) So erm. 

Interviewer:	What sort of things did he discuss with you when he came then?

Subject:	It’s just like what am I doing? Erm is my er, has the work from Uni been like useful? Or have you used it, like is anything wrong? Has anything happened? Er is there anything like that I need to tell him about? That sort of stuff, it was like how am I doing as well? 

Interviewer:	Did you tell him about the teasing and stuff?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	What did he say? 

Subject:	He says erm, I think it’s very, like just ignore it. But if it gets really bad then you should to speak to someone about it. Erm you know.

Interviewer:	Has it ever been bad enough, that you’ve felt like you needed to speak to someone then?

Subject:	Yeah. Yeah I wasn’t, it wasn’t teasing it was like something happened with this guy who but he’s like, he’s really, he’s one of those people like, who’s always in a bad mood and everything. He doesn’t mean that, to do anything, but he’s a little bit rude. And like, he’s very abrupt sometimes. You know it’s like, he knows the guys, don’t apologise. Then he, he did say he was sorry. Then I say, no that is written. And we talked about the way. He, and then said, go down there actually, since you, cos we’ve just moved offices. (Yep) Erm in the last month he’s actually been quite nice to me, but ...

Interviewer:	So did you go and speak to someone? 

Subject:	No. Because he’s a, a top manager. And I’m only a student, so. I don’t think it would bother them that much, you know. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Were you worried what the implications would be if you did go and speak to someone, if it would make it worse? 

Subject:	It might get, it might make it worse because, because one thing about this erm profession is. I don’t know if it’s just, just like here, you know, because I’ve never worked anywhere else, so I don’t really know. But gossip travels a lot, so if some one person knows about it, the whole site knows about it. So it, I think it would have made my situation worse. I told my boyfriend. And he said, oh you should tell someone. (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Did you speak to [name] about it?

Subject:	Yeah. And he asked me if he wanted to, if I wanted him to do anything about it? And I said no. 

Interviewer:	Oh. Is that who was prepared to if you? 

Subject:	Yes. Yes. If I wanted him to do something he would have. 

Interviewer:	Okay, did he speak to your supervisor or your line manager while he was here? 

Subject:	I think so. Oh yes he did, he spoke to erm the manager. (Yeah) Oh no, he was busy and he was in meetings, so I gave him his phone number and he like phoned him [inaudible].

Interviewer:	Are there appropriate facilities for women here? Toilets and safety clothing, things like that?

Subject:	Erm yeah. Is like, the (inaudible). Yeah, it’s like fine. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you still a career in engineering work? 

Subject:	I don’t want to be an engineer. So it won’t specifically be engineering, but in construction, yeah. 

Interviewer:	So your experiences haven’t put you off?

Subject:	No, it did put me off at the beginning, I was actually changing, I was thinking of changing my degree. But, erm no, not anymore. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that your experience here will help you cope when you do go to work after graduation? 

Subject:	Erm yes, definitely. 

Interviewer:	Would you work for [company] if they offered you a job when you finished? 

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	What will you look for in a company when you are looking for a job? 

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. I, well I think it’s (inaudible). I think it’s easy for a girl and jobs for erm (inaudible). But as a company I work for is, (inaudible). If you want to be, (inaudible) is a new company (inaudible). Because they’re like an international company and they’ve got to know (inaudible). It’s like loads of you can choose from where you want to go anyway. Whereas, (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Ok. I’ve just got a few questions I asked you last time now, to see if your opinion has changed since doing the placement. So, what five words would you use to describe the construction industry?

Subject:	Erm. It’s stressful. Demanding. You have to, I give er - er a strong will. Erm you have to be prepared to do like horrible sometimes, you can’t be all nicey nicey. And erm time management, you need be really good at organising and planning. You can’t leave everything to the last minute, you have to write everything down. (Yes) Draw big charts and diagrams and different (inaudible) check everything and, stuff like that. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged into engineering and construction?

Subject:	Yes but it doesn’t mean that they’re going to (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Do you think that anything could be done to change people’s attitudes? 

Subject:	Not unless they got like a woman’s head and a man’s body. No, you can’t have like have a, a, they have been known, it’s like erm one, which I knew of was like a woman who does scaffolding. And there’s one woman who does bricklaying. But it’s like a third of that, and you actually see it. (Right) But they have to be like really butch, I think. And it’s like something you can’t do. But like all the office stuff, like in management, that stuff, there probably should be more. (Okay) But I don’t know if there’s anything we should do to encourage them. Probably advertise them more. And give people opinions and. It does pay quite a bit, that’s the only reason why I like working in it, it pays more money. 

Interviewer:	Okay. What do you think are the main advantages and disadvantages of being a woman in a male dominated environment?

Subject:	You can use all my other examples here. Erm well, disadvantage, they swear a lot. They’ve got sex on the brain. It’s true er. Erm well it’s just erm. You have to be prepared to like talk to guys and like be around them, that kind of thing. Not be shy. Erm.

Interviewer:	Do you think it has made you more confident?

Subject:	Yeah you have to be really confident to speak to guys. Erm I can’t. (inaudible) I can’t think. 

Interviewer:	What about advantages?

Subject:	Working in a male dominated place, I don’t know really. Guys are all the same. And they do tend to ask you to make tea a lot. I mean, I said no, so many times, I’m not a receptionist. I mean it pissed me off quite a bit in the beginning, I’m not a receptionist. And it’s like, ‘oh love this blah blah blah. But then sometimes you like er, I mean like (inaudible). And sometimes like ah, he’s been nice but then, you don’t want to be treated like a guy sometimes. (Yeah) Which is like (inaudible). It’s like (inaudible). (Yeah) Erm.

Interviewer:	So do you feel like you have to act more like a guy to get on?

Subject:	I don’t want to do that, because I’ll just be called a lesbian.

Interviewer:	You don’t want to, but do you ever feel like you have to, to be accepted? 

Subject:	Sometimes you do. Yeah. You have to yes. Certainly you do have to act like a guy sometimes. I mean I’m not going to be like farting and things. (No) I mean, sometimes I can, like I do something, I think oh well that’s really. It’s a really guyish. And it’s like oh, you know. And you have, you have to. Sometimes. I can’t think of any other advantages. It’s just you, you get to relate more to guys, like if you. It uses for like other things, if you want to be like a manager and get a company. So they employ half girls, have guys. (Yeah) You can relate, you know is how, it teaches you how to handle guys that’s all. I mean you can handle the really bad ones and the really nice ones. So. I think that’s the main advantage. Yeah and guys are, come on to anything in a dress. Any girl walks past, short skirt on, well actually anything, any girl that walks passed, it’s like, they wolf whistle. It’s like, it’s oh. It’s like they’ve never ever seen a girl before. They’ve been like cooped up in some little shed somewhere and then they’ve been let out. (Yeah) Which is like, I just don’t understand it.

Interviewer:	I don’t envy you. 

Subject:	No, you don’t want to be an engineer. I mean I was an engineer for six months, I mean, it’s okay, yeah. But you go it’s pretty boring, there’s loads of maths, and working out, and you know. 

Interviewer:	Ok, that’s everything really. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Subject

(Yeah) So management, it’s like a management company, as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very useful (Yeah) You can’t, you can’t erm do my degree without doing placement. Definitely not. Unless you have started your degree and you were already working er, if you haven’t done anything before, if you’re eight - eighteen or something like that, you have to have a placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you using the skills that you’ve learnt at uni on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m not sure I’ve used anything. I know what everything means, that I have learnt and I have done all my coursework on. But, erm other than that, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So does that make you think what you’re doing at uni is a waste of time? Or do you still think it’s useful?
